Characterization and Utilization of the Elusive α,β-Unsaturated
N‑Tosyliminium: the Synthesis of Highly Functionalizable Skipped
Halo Enynes
Tapas R. Pradhan, Mukti Paudel, Jordan L. Harper, Paul Ha-Yeon Cheong, * and Jin Kyoon Park *
Cite This: Org. Lett. 2021, 23, 1427 −1433 Read Online
ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: A formal haloalkynylation of allenamides has been
described for the synthesis of highly stereo- and regioselective
skipped halo enynes. Exclusive γ-regioselectivity is achieved
through the intermediacy of a conjugated N-tosyliminium
intermediatedirect evidence for the formation of which was
validated by NMR and HRMS. Quantum mechanical computations
reveal that the reactive intermediate geometry is key to controlling
the 1,2- or 1,4-regioselectivity of alkyne interception. Divergent
access to elusive unsaturated systems has also been reported.
N-Acyliminium ions (NAIs), which are more electron-de ﬁcient
than the Mannich reagents, have been extensively employed in
the construction of alkaloids, natural compounds, and drug-like
molecules ( Scheme 1 A, right; synthetic routes to NAIs).
1
Recently, α,β-unsaturated NAIs have also been successfully
utilized in many selective additions and Diels −Alder reactions
for the synthesis of complex fused heterocycles. 2 Although the
N-sulfonyliminium ions have been relatively less exploited, 3 the
α,β-unsaturated analogue ions (i.e., of acyl and sulfonyl
iminiums) by various electrophilic activations are proposed
as potential intermediates to explain unique regio- and
stereoselectivity in recent allenamide chemistry ( Scheme 1 A,
left).
4 Despite vast applications of the iminium ions by
trapping with nucleophiles, neither α,β-unsaturated N-
acyliminium nor N-sulfonyliminium ions have been spectro-
scopically observed, presumably due to high reactivity and
instability, to our knowledge. 4k Notably, the ﬁrst precedent in
the detection of NAIs, generated from α-alkoxycarbamates
using BF3·OEt2, by NMR was reported in 1992 by Yamamoto
et al. 5
1,n-Enynes are important synthetic building blocks in
modern organic synthesis with many elegant methods for
their preparation, as well as great versatility, which allows for
ready diversi ﬁcation into other functional groups.
6 Alkynyla-
tion of alkynes or allenes 7,8 is a well-established method for the
generation of 1, n-enynes since the ﬁrst discovery by Trost in
1990,8a and several catalytic variants have also been reported
for the synthesis of 1,3- or 1,4-enynes. 9 A direct synthetic
approach to ﬂuorinated skipped enynes via hydroalkynylation
of gem-diﬂuorinated cyclopropanes has also recently been
reported by Fu. 10 In the context of adding haloalkynes into
unsaturated C −C bonds, Jiang reported Pd(II)-catalyzed
haloalkynylation cross-coupling reactions of internal alkynes
and cycloalkenes. 11,12
We recently reported a ligand-controlled strategy for the
regio- and stereodivergent synthesis of 1,3- or 1,4-enynamides
from allenamides ( Scheme 1 B).13 Continuing to pursue the
selective synthesis of functionalizable 1,4-enynamides, we
hypothesized that nucleophilic alkynes could trap the α,β-
unsaturated N-tosyliminium ion known to be generated from
allenamides and N-halosuccinimides;4d−i no fruitful results
were witnessed however, although cases involving the
intermediacy of such α,β-unsaturated N-tosyliminium ions
are proposed in many selective addition reactions to
allenamides such as haloimidation, 4d haloamination,4e hal-
oalkoxylation,4f and haloarylation. 4h Careful screening for the
creation of α,β-unsaturated N-tosyliminium ion reactive
intermediates using various N,O-aminal adducts and Lewis
acids reveals the ﬁrst NMR and HRMS detection of A, which
was generated from the reaction of 2a and BF 3·OEt2, and
followed by successful trapping with a catalytically generated
alkynylzinc species (Scheme 1C).14 The successful detection of
A is attributed to the stable “ate” complex formation of
nucleophilc benzoic acid with BF 3 (see Figure 2 ).
Our investigation commenced with the screening of various
diﬀerent N,O-aminals ( 2), obtained by reacting allenesulfona-
mide 1 with NBS and acid or alcohol, 15 with phenyl acetylene

(3a) under Lewis acidic conditions using metal salt ( Scheme
2).16 After thorough screening, we found that the reaction of
2a with ZnBr2 (10 mol %), BF 3·OEt2 (1.1 equiv), and Hu ̈nig’s
base (2.5 equiv) gave the highest yield of 4aa in 94% isolated
yield with exclusive Z-selectivity (see Supporting Information
for details of stereochemistry assignment). γ-Alkynylation
product 4aa using acetate-counterpart 2a-iii was isolated in
73% yield, outcompeting the α-alkynylation product (entry 2).
Further screening using other α-bromo- N-sulfonyl- N,O-
aminals ( 2a−i and 2a-ii) including α-halo-N,O-aminals ( 2a-
iv to 2a-vi) under identical conditions did not reveal a good
overall yield of 4aa in comparison to aminal ( 2a) having a
benzoate leaving group (entries 1, 3, and 4). Control
experiments showed that subtracting either reagent, including
deviation of their equivalent amount, is not bene ﬁcial (entries
5−10). The attempt to employ Li-acetylide was futile, yielding
an intractable mixture of compounds (entry 11). A sequential
one-pot reaction gave a poor yield (33%) presumably due to
the residual imide; however, its removal by basic workup
doubled the overall yield of 4aa (entry 12). As expected, the
controlled experiments without Zn-salt or Hu ̈nig’s base did not
provide 4aa (entry 13).
With reaction conditions optimized, we next investigated the
scope of alkyne coupling partners 3 (Scheme 3) and are happy
to report that a broad substrate scope for both aryl and
aliphatic alkynes are tolerated. The reaction is also tolerant of a
variety of substituents located in various positions on the aryl
rings, a ﬀording the analogous halo enynamides ( 4aa−4ai)i n
up to 95% yield ( Scheme 3 A). Of note is that the reaction
tolerates halogenated alkynes (F and Cl), enabling the
synthesis of halo enynes with easily modi ﬁable reaction sites.

Bromoalkynylation to form 4aa was e ﬃciently scaled up to 5
mmol scale, and the product was obtained in 96% yield
without chromatographic puri ﬁcation. Heteroaryl alkyne 3j is
also a suitable substrate for this transformation, as are simple
aliphatic alkynes ( 3k, 3l), strained ring alkynes ( 3m), and 1,3-
enyne ( 3n), which all smoothly gave the expected products in
good yields ( 4ak−n). Silylated alkynes ( 3o, 3p) also gave the
desired products ( 4ao−p) in moderate yields, although a
slightly extended time is required in comparison with other
alkynes. This result is likely due to β-carbocationic stabilization
by the proximal silyl functional group. Other acid- or base-
sensitive functional groups including benzyl-, silyl-, and
benzoyl-protected propargylic alcohols ( 3q−3s), were also
well tolerated, highlighting the versatility of this reaction for
modiﬁcation of hydroxyl-based moieties.
The requirements of allenic substituents to have a group for
eﬀective electronic balance around the allenic skeleton were
more rigid, and we noticed that it is essential for γ-selective
alkynylation ( Scheme 4 ). In addition to the tosyl group ( 1a
and 1b
17), cyclic amide groups were also viable, giving the
corresponding γ-alkynylation product ( 4ca) in good yield.
Moreover, both cyclic and acyclic carbamate substituents did
not a ﬀect the stereo- and regioselectivity of the product ( 4da,
4ea), which further imitates the predictable electronic bias

seen with sulfonyl substituents ( Scheme 4A). To further probe
the substituent e ﬀect controlling the γ-regioselectivity, we
subjected N,O-aminals of allenamine 1f (carbazole bearing
bulkier N-substituent) and allenyl ether 1g without any
electron-withdrawing group (EWG), to our bromo-alkynyla-
tion conditions ( Scheme 4 B). Interestingly, mixtures of
nonisolable regioisomeric products were obtained (with an
α-alkynylation product as the major product for the Br-
substituent and exclusive one for the I-substituent), signifying
the requirement of a suitable electron biasing element on the
nitrogen atom to achieve the γ-regioselectivity. While attempts
to functionalize other allene derivatives such as those bearing a
nitrile (1h), phosphine oxide ( 1i), o-tosyl (1j), and one carbon
homologated allenyl ether ( 1k) failed ( Scheme 4 C). This
process was nonetheless amenable to the use of other halogens
(Cl, I) with chloro- and iodo-alkynylation products obtained in
good yields, albeit slightly longer reaction times were required
for 5b indicating the halo participation is a reasonable
proposition ( Scheme 4 D). A substituted allenamide 1l led to
a vinylogous elimination product 6
17 (Scheme 4 E).
To discover the origins of the observed regioselectivity, we
turned to computations. 18 We ﬁrst computed the ground state
oxazolidinone and carbazole allenamide substrates and their
halogenated reactive intermediates ( Figure 1 ),
19 speciﬁcally
the C1 −C2 chloroniums, the C2 −C3 chloroniums, and the
vinyl chloride-iminiums. C1−C2 Chloroniums for both
oxazolidinone- and carbazole-derived allenes spontaneously
decomposed to vinyl chlorides, and the C2−C3 Chloroniums
were energetically unreasonable ( ΔG > 40 kcal/mol). In
contrast, the vinyl chloride iminiums of them were found to be
energetically accessible. These results suggest that the vinyl
chloride iminiums are operative reactive intermediates in these
reactions, not the chloronium ions. The possibility of halogen
bonds was also probed for all these intermediates where
geometrically possible, and in our hands, such interactions did
not substantively improve the stabilities.
To acquire experimental validation of these computational
analyses, NMR studies were then conducted for the benzoic
acid derived N,O-aminal 2a and methanol-derived N,O-aminal
2a−v adducts ( Figure 2 ). To our surprise, we were able to
successfully elucidate the sulfonyl iminium structure at room
temperature for the ﬁrst time. In the case of 2a, after treatment
of 1.1 equiv of BF
3·OEt2 at room temperature, the appearance
of a new peak at 9.25 ppm and the down ﬁeld shifting of both
vinylic protons from 5.73 and 5.91 ppm to 6.91 ppm clearly
indicate the formation of the iminium species. The analogous
experiment involving 2a−v resulted in a complex spectrum,
revealing the highly reactive nature of the iminium derived
from the corresponding N,O-aminal 2a−v. This is presumably
due to the more Lewis basic nature of the methoxide
counterion compared to the benzoate counterion in the case
of 2a. The stability and the existence of the sulfonyl iminium
intermediates were further corroborated through the appear-
ance of m/z peaks in ESI-HRMS, corresponding to both
isotopic molecular ions.
The regioselectivity of nucleophilic addition may be
explained by the ground state conformations of the vinyl
chloride iminiums. The vinyl chloride of the oxazolidinone
iminium is planar at 179 ° and conjugated, while the vinyl
chloride of the carbazole iminium is signi ﬁcantly bent out of
planarity at >40 ° and out of conjugation. In the carbazoles, the
steric repulsion between the vinyl chloride and the fused
benzene prevents them from achieving planarity. These
structures suggest therefore that the carbazole iminiums
would most likely undergo 1,2 nucleophilic additions, while
the oxazolidinone iminium would prefer 1,4 additions. Indeed,
computed transition structures were in agreement with these
observation and hypotheses. The carbazole iminium preferred
to undergo 1,2-addition over the 1,4 by 1.5 kcal/mol, and in
contrast, the oxazolidinone iminium preferred to undergo a
1,4-conjugate addition by 9.2 kcal/mol ( Figure 3 ).
20 The
computed selectivity values were in agreement with experi-
ments, where the oxazolidinone additions gave exclusively 1,4
addition, whereas the carbazole additions gave a mixture.
Moreover, the oxazolidinone has a signi ﬁcantly lower addition
barrier by 4.6 kcal/mol compared to the carbazole, matching
experiments that showed the additions of the former were
rapid whereas the latter were sluggish.

The synthetic applicability of this method can be easily
exploited, illustrated, for example, in Scheme 5 . In employing
propargylic ethers as the alkyne coupling partner, bromo
enynamides 4at and 4au were synthesized in acceptable yields,
which showcases the late-stage diversi ﬁcation of natural
products
L-(+)-menthol and cholesterol ( Scheme 5A). Further
synthetic transformations can also be achieved, as shown in
Scheme 5 B: 4aa was smoothly transformed into allene
enamide ( 7) via organic base (Et
3N) mediated isomerization
and skipped diynamide ( 8) through inorganic base (K tOBu)
mediated dehydrohalogenation ( Scheme 5 B-i and -ii).
Interestingly, a one-pot base-induced isomerization and 4 π-
electrocyclization enabled synthesis of cyclobutene amide 9
(Scheme 5 B-iii), the structure of which was con ﬁrmed by X-
ray crystallography (CCDC number: 2019531). Furthermore,
semi- and full-reduction of 4aa using Lindlar ’s catalyst were
also feasible to selectively hydrogenate the C C triple bond
furnishing 10 and 11, while keeping intact the enamide
unsaturation (Scheme 5 B-iv and -v). Notably, the C −Br bond
of 4aa could be modi ﬁed to allene appended conjugated
ynenamide ( 12) through a one-pot two-step transformation,
and arylated-skipped ynenamide ( 13), by stereospeci ﬁc Suzuki
coupling ( Scheme 5 B-vi and vii).
In summary, an e ﬃcient formal haloalkynylation protocol
has been reported. Studies on the electronic e ﬀects of N-
substituents shows that the haloalkynylation process occurs
through electronic cooperation with a neighboring halogen,
thus enabling γ-selective interception of an alkynyl-nucleophile
via generation of electrophilic vinyl halide species. More
importantly, the intriguing functionalities of halo enynes pave
the way to synthesize unsaturated synthons which can be
further functionalized with ease.
